#10517. 23 ways to handle tasks that trigger dread

Everyone has them: Tasks they dread. They can range from mundane or routine items that clog the calendar to difficult conversations and meetings that cause stress. Avoiding them doesn’t make them go away. It just makes the dread heavier. Figuring out how to get through them frees up the time and headspace they take up. 

We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they handle tasks they dread. Here, 23 of them provide their best tips for getting them off your to-do list.

1. BODY-DOUBLE THE TASK

I don’t tackle them alone. We call it body doubling: pulling in a teammate for a focused session to knock out the task neither of us wants to face solo. It depends on the task at hand too! My default is our incredible chief of staff. She’s the left brain to my right brain. From there it’s our executive team if the task requires finance, operations, technology, etc. Consistently routing the task with the right team members keeps the business moving forward. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will

2. JUST DO IT AND DO IT NOW

Dread is what you feel when you aren’t just doing it. Just do it. And when you do, more often than not you enter flow state, and you just keep doing stuff. — Eric Simons, Bolt.new

3. APPROACH IT LIKE AN ATHLETE

When I face a task I’d rather avoid, I try to tackle it right away, before I give myself a hundred reasons to postpone it. I approach these situations like an athlete: Discomfort is part of progress, not a reason to stop. Whether it’s a challenging negotiation or a difficult decision, I’ve learned to take action even when I don’t feel ready. Years of daily training and building at my company have taught me that motivation comes and goes, and discipline is the key to keeping you moving forward. You can’t always control how you feel about a task, but you can train yourself to show up and get it done anyway. — Victoria Repa, BetterMe

4. TAKE ONE SMALL STEP

In my mind, most dread comes from a task that has no clear definition or parameter. I’ve found it helpful to jump on the first physical step, small enough to finish in a few minutes (e.g., open the file, draft the subject line, pull last month’s numbers) and physically stop there to build next steps. This creates a sense of internal accountability. Once the task has a shape, the rest usually goes faster than the dread predicted. Also, if it still sits there after a week, that’s useful information: It may belong to someone else, or it may not need doing at all. — James Chester, WVN

5. CHIP AWAY EACH DAY

Momentum beats motivation. I start small and chip away a little each day. Procrastinating doesn’t buy you time, it just weighs you down, and eventually it crowds out the work you love. — Tami Rosen, executive board and advisor to technology and finance companies

6. TACKLE THEM FIRST, EARLY IN THE DAY

I do them first, and I make them smaller. Dread grows in the gap between knowing a task needs doing and starting it. So I close that gap early in the day, before anything else competes for my attention. If it’s big, I commit only to the first part. Momentum handles the rest. I’ve also learned to ask what the dread is telling me. Sometimes it’s a sign the task needs a conversation, not more effort, and the fastest way through is a call to the right person. — Megan Noel, Covista

7. NAME WHAT YOU DREAD AND WHY

Usually, people dread something because it is uncomfortable, ambiguous, or carries some sort of emotional weight. I try to name what I dread and why, instead of pretending the task itself is the problem. If it matters, do it and do it now, because avoidance compounds just like progress does. The things we put off usually get heavier, not lighter. — Ethan Braden, Texas A&M University

8. TAKE OUT THE TRASH DAY

A colleague once inspired me with her “take out the trash day,” dedicating a chunk of time each week to knock through dreaded tasks. With all the noise on Slack, texts, and email, I block an hour at the end of the week, mute my notifications, and cruise through. It’s how I take care of budgets, expenses, and the general paperwork, so I can get back to the creative work where I’m in my flow. Sometimes there’s a snack reward waiting at the end. — Courtney Brigham, Typeface

9. SET A REWARD FOR YOURSELF

I break it down into chunks, set a target date and time to complete each chunk, and then block out time and get it done. I also set a reward for myself after doing it. For example, I’ll get to have this great lunch after I finish it. It sounds silly, but it’s nice to have rewards after doing a project that is not enjoyable! — Felicia Curcuru, Binti

10. RELY ON PREPARATION

During dreaded high-stakes situations like meetings with multiple stakeholders or delivering sensitive performance-based feedback, I rely on preparation. Coming armed with a brief outline of mission-critical points ensures you stay on track and helps you recover if the conversation gets derailed. If I’m ruminating on a complex problem that I just can’t seem to crack, I put everything down and do something completely unrelated. Taking a walk, listening to a podcast, or even washing the dishes allows my brain to marinate, discover hidden connections, and eventually the solution becomes clear. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners

11. PRIORITIZE ACCORDINGLY

Tasks I dread are rarely the most important for our business, so I prioritize them accordingly. However, they tend to bubble up to the higher end of the list of less critical tasks. The longer they remain on my to-do list, the more days they get to impact my morale, so I’m motivated to get them done. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps

12. CONNECT IT TO OUTCOME

I try to stay positive by focusing on the value the task will create once it’s completed. I put it in the broader context of the goal it supports and the impact it will have. As a big-picture person, details can be challenging, but connecting the work to a meaningful outcome helps me stay motivated and push through with a positive mindset. — Chris K Bailey, Bailey Brand Consulting

13. TAKE THE MEDICINE ALL AT ONCE

I put them off. Then I bundle them up and take care of them all at once. Like medicine. It tastes bad but works. Sort of like Buckley’s cough and cold medicine. — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

14. STOP AND MAP IT OUT

If I catch myself spending real time on something where I’m just going through the motions, I stop and map it out. What are the inputs, what am I doing with them, and what does the output need to look like? Once the process is clearly mapped, it’s usually pretty obvious that a lot of it doesn’t need me. Then I build an automation around it. I still get the result; I just skip the mundane part. — Mike Sewell, Gresham Smith

15. ASK WHETHER YOU’RE THE RIGHT PERSON TO DO IT

I try not to spend too much time negotiating with myself. If something needs to be done, I focus on the next step and start. Usually, the anticipation is worse than the task itself. As a CEO, I’ve also learned to ask whether I’m the right person to do it. There are many things I can do, but I don’t need to do all of them. Sometimes leadership means taking something on yourself. Other times it means trusting someone else to own it. What I try to avoid is letting something I don’t enjoy become something the organization has to wait for. — Yuping Huang, Quantum Computing Inc.

16. CARVE UP YOUR DAY

Technology marketing is constant context switching and rapid decision-making. If you’re not careful, a whole day passes without a minute of real thought or creativity. You give in to the “critical” transactions, and eventually the work that’s most critical to your job disappears entirely. So I carve up my day. Mornings are for content, strategy, and creative problem-solving. Midday is the transactional work. The last couple of hours go to administration and anything that wasn’t urgent. And if something that needs real creativity slips through until late in the day, it gets the first look the next morning, with fresh eyes. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr

17. DIVIDE IT INTO MANAGEABLE STEPS

When I face a task I dread, I focus on understanding what makes it difficult and what depends on completing it. This matters because postponing an uncomfortable responsibility does not remove it. It can affect decisions, relationships, and other people’s work. I divide the task into manageable steps, establish a clear deadline, and begin with the first action. For me, discipline is not about enjoying every responsibility. It is about addressing what needs to be done before hesitation becomes a larger problem. — Manuel Freire-Garabal, Gioya HEI

18. DO THE WORST THING FIRST

Do it first. I was told once that you should always do the worst thing on your to-do list first because the day then only gets better. Have stuck to it ever since. And never overlook the power of reward: For every annoying task give yourself a little treat in return. The promise of a future good thing coming your way works every time. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo

19. AUTOMATE THE MUNDANE

Recently, I’ve unlocked a new cheat code in chipping away at those dreaded tasks. When walking to work, I’ll start talking with my favorite large language model of the moment and we can hammer out 10 open items from unanswered Slack messages and emails to meeting recaps and other nagging tasks that can quickly pile up. When all the right connectors are in place, the efficiency unlock is tremendous and has been a game changer for knocking out those dreaded to-dos. — Matt Conlin, Fluent

20. KNOW WHEN THE TASK BELONGS TO SOMEONE ELSE

I like to understand every aspect of my business, even the things that don’t come naturally to me. I’m always open to learning something new, but I also recognize when something falls outside my skill set. I believe in knowing your strengths and surrounding yourself with people who bring expertise you don’t have. If it’s something I can tackle, I get it done. If someone else can do it better, I delegate. My time is best spent where I can make the greatest impact. — Kim Wileman, No Makeup Makeup

21. USE THE HEADWIND AS A TAILWIND

I once heard Jimmy Iovine, co-founder of Beats, talk about using a headwind as a tailwind, and it’s stuck with me ever since. If there’s something you hate doing, run towards it, not away from it. Delay is a false economy because it just extends the dread. Then I break it into tiny actions and get the first one done. Momentum beats motivation every time, and most tasks are never as bad as the story you’ve told yourself about them. — Emily Kortlang, Meaco

22. MEET IT AT YOUR COGNITIVE PEAK

I use power hours. I know my brain is sharpest late in the evening or early in the morning, so I save the tasks I would normally procrastinate on for that window. I don’t do it every day. The idea is simple: Dreaded work takes far less energy when you meet it at your cognitive peak, so an hour or two of focus can clear what would otherwise linger for weeks. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards

23. ATTACK THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES

I try to attack the first five minutes rather than the whole task. Dread grows in the space between knowing you have to do something and starting it. Once I take action, the task usually gets a lot less intimidating. — Ran Mullins, Psympl

#10515. Is another crypto winter upon us? Why Bitcoin, XRP, and Ethereum fell more than 20% in a month

The crypto markets are down again today, with major tokens suffering significant losses over the past 30 days.

As of this writing, Bitcoin is trading below $65,000, Ethereum is nearly down to $1,800, and XRP is below 96 cents.

Those are more than 20%, 25%, and 26% drops, respectively, over the past month.

Bitcoin hit an all-time high of more than $126,000 a token in October 2025, meaning its value has roughly halved since then.

Those falls are causing some to wonder whether another crypto winter is upon us. The term describes extended bear markets across cryptocurrencies, in which digital tokens drop significantly in value and stay down. Major crypto winters previously hit in 2018–2019 and 2022–2023. 

It may be too early to tell whether this is the start of another one, but several factors have been driving cryptocurrencies lower in recent weeks. Here’s what you need to know.

Expected Federal Reserve interest rate hikes

One of the greatest factors likely weighing on cryptocurrencies is the expectation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December. As Reuters reported, a majority of economists expect the Fed to hike rates next month. The hike is expected to be by 25 basis points, to a range of 4.00%–4.25%.

Rate hikes make money more expensive to borrow. This can encourage people to save, which can dampen spending and thus help fight inflation.

But when money is more expensive to borrow, those who lend it can earn more. So, when rates are higher, investors tend to pull their money from non-interest-bearing assets, like crypto, and put it into interest-bearing assets like U.S. Treasury bills.

This reallocation leads to a selloff in crypto, driving the basket of digital currencies lower.

AI stock rut

Cryptocurrencies aren’t the only assets having a tough time lately.

Big Tech stocks—especially AI-adjacent ones—are having a rough few weeks. Last week was perhaps the worst thanks to the Jensen Huang scandal that sent shares of Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) down more than 12% during the last five trading days.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq is also down about 1% during the same period.

AI stocks and cryptocurrencies often tend to move in tandem. Both are highly volatile and act as speculative assets. When one falls, investors tend to get jittery and sell off the other class in an effort to prevent further losses and lock in gains.

The 2026 midterm elections

A blue tsunami swept across America in early November’s midterm elections. In some ways, that is very good for the markets, as a large political majority brings a certain amount of certainty.

Investors may or may not like that party’s policy positions—but knowing what’s coming can help them plan financially.

Unfortunately for crypto, the incoming Democratic Congress may be much less friendly to the industry.

Crypto investors fear that this new political leadership could propose stronger regulation, which may stymie the industry’s growth—or at least impose checks it otherwise wouldn’t have had if the GOP had retained control of Congress.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index falls to “Extreme Fear” level

Unsurprisingly, after a 20-plus percent selloff in major tokens over the past month, investors are fretting about crypto’s future—at least in the near term. 

And nowhere is that worry more evident than when you take a look at CoinMarketCap’s Crypto Fear and Greed Index. The index tracks investor sentiment surrounding the crypto markets. It ranges from 0 to 100.

The higher the index, the more optimistic (and potentially greedy) investors tend to be about Bitcoin and other tokens. The lower the index, the more fearful they tend to be.

Right now, the index stands at a paltry 13, placing it in the “Extreme Fear” range—its lowest range. It has not been at this level since February 2026, when Bitcoin fell from around $87,500 to around $60,000 in the first few days of the month.

Of course, despite the index’s low rating—and the many factors weighing crypto down over the past month—it’s still too early to tell whether the crypto markets are on the cusp of another prolonged downturn. But the longer the rout lasts, the more the specter of another crypto winter will weigh on investors’ minds.

#10513. Technical Aspects of AI-Generated Video Assets for Web Design

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

#10512. Nike spent years reinventing Air. Meet the new Tuned Air (exclusive)

For half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air. The cushioning—developed at NASA, then incorporated inside a 1978 running shoe and the Air Max 1—came to represent Nike’s commitment to cutting-edge innovation. Now, with Nike on its back foot after several years of missteps, the company is counting on a new version of Air to help pull it out of its slump.

Today, a day before it announces its financial results, Nike is unveiling Tuned Air, a high-tech evolution of Air that has been in the works for years. It’s debuting this technology in a running sneaker that will come out within a year. But Nike sees Tuned Air as a broader platform that can be incorporated into other sports and even its apparel lines.

It’s one way Nike hopes to restore its credibility as an innovator and win back runners who have drifted to rivals. Given how much ground Nike has lost in recent years, it’s unclear whether this strategy will work. But the company is optimistic.

“There’s no better innovation that speaks to our formula than Air,” says Phil McCartney, Nike’s chief innovation, design, and product officer.

McCartney has spent three decades at Nike, where he ran the footwear business from 2016 until last year, when CEO Elliott Hill put him in charge of innovation, design and product across Nike, Jordan, and Converse. Speaking to me from the LeBron James Innovation Center at Nike’s campus in Beaverton, Oregon, McCartney explained that his team has a motto borrowed from two Nike legends: “Create epic shit. Make athletes better.” (The first comes from Kobe Bryant, the second from Nike’s cofounder, Bill Bowerman.)

McCartney says Nike is translating that slogan into a formula, “athlete, science, solution,” that will guide the company’s approach to innovation. His teams gather insights from athletes, then tests ideas at the Nike Sports Research Lab in Beaverton and through field teams in Eldoret, Kenya; London, and Shanghai.

Introducing Nike Tuned Air

The original Air technology created tough pockets of nitrogen using two sheets of plastic. In that case, the air was evenly distributed, creating cushioning throughout the pocket. With Tuned Air, Nike adds nuance. Before the plastic sheets are pressed together, Nike adds a chemical that allows it to create a pattern; it can now fine-tune where the gas is located and how much air is in each pocket. In doing so, it can make one part of the cushion soft and springy, and another part firm and stable. “It allows us to completely change the relationship between cushioning and support, and precision-tune the experience,” says McCartney.

Nike has given this technology to runners over the last few years. “The feedback that we’ve had from the runners who have been trying this for a couple of years now is it feels like no other cushioning system out there,” he says. “Incredibly well cushioned, but also has stability. That’s the sort of holy grail that we’ve been trying to unlock in Air.”

While Nike’s approach to achieving this balance might be distinct, many other running brands are also trying to balance cushioning with structure with their own innovations. Brooks’s DNA Tuned foam uses a dual-cell construction, with large cells in the heel to cushion landings and smaller cells in the front to make the toes more responsive. Hoka’s H-Frame features a firm strip of foam in the midsole, surrounded by softer cushioning. On’s CloudTec technology uses hollow tubes of foam molded to the bottom of the sole to absorb impact, along with a steel plate in the midsole.

With this newfound ability to modulate how much air is in each pocket, Nike can now explore “wildly different expressions” of the technology, McCartney says. Besides running, Tuned Air will be incorporated into other sports, like soccer, and into clothing like the Air Milano jacket, creating air pockets that improve temperature regulation.

Nike can even integrate Tuned Air into lifestyle shoes, like vintage sneakers, creating more comfort. “How could we make an Air Force 1 using a sock liner that is Tuned Air, so you get comfort and support?” McCartney says.

Nike has streamlined the manufacturing of Tuned Air so that it can move 70% faster than it typically does from idea to product. This is crucial to allowing Nike to be nimble as it seeks to compete with the many rivals that are also spinning out innovative new products quickly.

Nike Needs a Win

Nike needs this innovation to resonate with consumers. Last quarter, revenue declined 4% to $11.2 billion, and the company expects full-year sales to fall by a high single digit percentage. Sportswear, which accounts for nearly half the business, fell by double digits. Sales in China dropped 26% and Converse sank 28%. Nike has announced a restructuring plan that will cut more jobs after several rounds of layoffs in recent years.

Nike’s rivals have been closely observing its missteps, and taken advantage of the opportunity to steal market share. In running, a category Nike once dominated, it’s now in third place, trailing Brooks and Hoka. In the lifestyle sphere, Adidas has had hit after hit by bringing back its classic Samba and Gazelle, and New Balance has turned its retro styles like the 550 into bestsellers. Meanwhile, Nike hasn’t had a lifestyle sneaker hit in years.

Nike’s running business is starting to recover. It’s grown by double digits for more than a year, helped by the successful Vomero line. “We’re seeing market share gains almost daily right now,” says McCartney.

Historically, Nike has built running technology for elite athletes that tries to shave seconds off on their race times. But that technology takes a long time to trickle down into running shoes that the average person can lace up.

Nike doesn’t have the luxury of time anymore. That’s why its Tuned Air is designed for the everyday runner. “The entry point will be that everyday run,” McCartney says. “When you’re just trying to log your Tuesday morning run, you want the maximum amount of running with precision-tuned support.”

Nike is making a big bet on Tuned Air. But whether enough consumers get excited about the technology—and the forthcoming sneakers—to boost Nike’s fortunes is unclear. Tomorrow, when Nike lays out its long-term financial plans, we’ll get a better glimpse into how much ground it has yet to make up.

#10510. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#10508. Santa with a cause: Amazon Prime teams up with Arnold Schwarzenegger for its latest holiday campaign

After more than five decades in Hollywood, Arnold Schwarzenegger finally feels fit to play his most iconic role yet. And he’s taking the reins just in time for the holiday season.

The Terminator and Total Recall actor is suiting up in bright red and white for Amazon Prime’s new holiday creative campaign, “Santa Schwarzenegger,” which debuts on Monday.

The advertising spot begins with Schwarzenegger looking a little forlorn as the paparazzi chase him around New York. He then orders a Santa suit from Prime, allowing for anonymity as Schwarzenegger donates snacks to a dog rescue center, watches a basketball game, and heaves a Christmas tree onto the roof of a car.

“I’m at that age now and it’s believeable”

Throughout his career, Schwarzenegger has played plenty of iconic roles. He’s portrayed a killing machine from the future, Batman’s nemesis Mr. Freeze, both Hercules and his father, Zeus, and an undercover cop teaching kindergarteners.

But Schwarzenegger says no role he has ever played has been as worldwide as this one.

“This is the perfect time for me to play Santa, because I’m at that age now and it’s more believable,” Schwarzenegger tells Fast Company. “With all the interesting characters that I played in my career—from Conan to Terminator—I thought that Santa is the ultimate.”

For Amazon, the Schwarzenegger spot fits neatly into two goals: driving sales and attention to Prime, a core pillar of the online retail giant’s Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and other holiday sales events throughout the season.

But it also ties in neatly with Amazon Prime’s The Man with the Bag, an upcoming holiday film that debuts on December 2, starring Schwarzenegger as Santa for a second time.

Alan Ritchson, Awkwafina, and Ken Jeong are also featured in the film’s cast. The film also ties into Amazon’s 2026 holiday campaign, which is called “Joy Delivered.”

“Arnold is the king of the kids, we saw that when he made Kindergarten Cop,” Jo Shoesmith, Amazon’s vice president and global chief brand officer, tells Fast Company. “There is a warmth and charm to him that lives outside of the character of Santa.”

Santa “has to be in shape”

“Santa Schwarzenegger” will run through December 23 across several channels including television, digital, social, and streaming audio. Yet another component of the campaign that Amazon is promoting is Schwarzenegger’s curated holiday gift guide, which includes plush dog toys, supplements, toys intended for children and grandchildren, and dumbbells.

“Think about it, Santa has to fly all the way from the North Pole, he has to be in shape to hand out the gifts at every single continent to go to every single house,” says Schwarzenegger. “It is a lot of work. He has to be in shape.” 

There are also two books: Better Every Day, a self-help book penned by Schwarzenegger that’s due to be published in January, and Arnold, which is written about him.

There’s also a cigar lighter, which may seem counterintuitive for the fitness enthusiast, but apparently he’s smoked them for over 40 years, including during his interview with Fast Company.

“We never want to twist the arm of the personality to put something in their mouth that doesn’t come across as authentic,” says Shoesmith. “It’s very driven by his holiday ordering list.” 

As an Austrian, Schwarzenegger says his holiday traditions differed from how he raised his children in America. The holiday is celebrated on December 24 and the gift giver is a baby Jesus called Christkind, not Santa, though Schwarzenegger says the latter has become more popular there in recent years. 

“I always question with every script I get: is this something that would just be good for America, or just good for Europe, or is this something that can play in every continent,” says Schwarzenegger.

Santa, he says, is a role that can “entertain the whole world.”

The rise of star-powered Santas

While Santa has been “the face” of the Christmas holiday for marketers for more than a century, the celebrity angle has been a more recent development.

John Travolta has played the role in multiple ad spots for Capital One, while Jon Hamm did so for Fox Sports, Steve Carell for Comcast, and Brent Bailey for Target.

“He’s kind of just this joyous, universally loved figure,” adds Shoesmith. To be clear, Shoesmith was talking about Schwarzenegger at this moment, not Santa, though she says both have cross-generational appeal.

Schwarzenegger is also a safe casting choice for the retailer at a time when the American consumer isn’t optimistic. Unease about the economy was a central theme in the recent midterm elections, and the sales projection forecasts for the upcoming holiday season look fairly mixed.

Research firm Circana says average holiday spending will total $779 this year, down from $796 in 2025. The trade association the National Retail Federation is more bullish, expecting retail sales in November and December to increase 4.2% to about $1 trillion, compared to a year ago.

“We’re a brand whose logo is a smile, so joy is inherently part of who we are as a brand,” says Shoesmith of the tone approach for Amazon Prime’s campaign. “We really make sure that we have a great selection of brands at a really great price, and that’s really important for customers right now . . . they’re very price conscious.”

#10506. What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.

But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.

Officials say no connection to ground stop

The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.

The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”

But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”

SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.

What is the SMART system?

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.

The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.

The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.

So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.

According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.

SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.

Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”

To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.

No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.

Concerns around relying on AI

While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.

Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”

The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”

“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”

He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”

The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.

In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.

“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

—Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk, Associated Press

#10504. Trump’s tariffs will be tough to defeat, despite Democrats’ landslide in the midterms. Here’s why

For months, Democrats on the campaign trail hammered President Donald Trump’s unpopular tariffs, arguing that the taxes on imports drive up prices for American families already frustrated by the high cost of living.

James Talarico, a Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, blamed Trump’s tariff on Mexican tomatoes for pushing up the price of a popular appetizer: “Chips and salsa,” he said, “are sacred in Texas.”

Targeting tariffs proved to be a winning message nationwide, contributing to the Democrats’ stunning gains in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. And in Texas? Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1988.

“Americans don’t like tariffs,” said Scott Lincicome at the Cato Institute’s Center for Trade Policy Studies. “They connect them to the cost of living.”

But when the Democrats take full control of Congress, they are likely to find that reversing Trump’s tariffs won’t be easy.

The president will still have power to veto any legislation that repeals his import taxes or reins in his legal authority to impose them. And it’s unclear — probably doubtful — that enough Republicans would defy Trump and join Democrats in overriding his veto.

Moreover, Democrats themselves are divided over trade policy. Some want to move back toward low-tariff trade policies that Trump demolished. Other Democrats want to see the United States continue using tariffs to fight other countries’ unfair trade policies and to sanction U.S. adversaries such as China.

“There’s going to be a big debate over what should the Democrats’ tariff and trade policy be,” said Ryan Majerus, a former U.S. trade official during Trump’s first term and in the Biden administration. “It can’t just be: We don’t like what Trump’s doing.”

Complicating matters is the fact that Trump’s tariffs are delivering significant amounts of revenue to the U.S. Treasury — nearly $370 billion in the last two budget years — at a time when the federal government is sitting on a staggering $40 trillion in debt.

Democrats have “just been elected to come in and address concerns about affordability,” said Sally Laing, former chief trade counsel for the Senate Finance Committee and now a partner at the law firm Akin Gump. “It’s not as easy as people may think.”

Trump’s tariffs pinched family budgets

The U.S. Constitution gives the power to levy taxes — including tariffs — to Congress. But over the years, lawmakers have relinquished tariff-setting authority to the president.

Trump swept into the vacuum. In his first term, he started a trade war with China and slapped taxes on steel and aluminum imports, saying they posed a threat to U.S. national security. All that was just a warmup for his second term. Although the Supreme Court rejected his most ambitious tariffs in February, he has still managed to build a high protective wall around the U.S. economy, sometimes relying on the expansive use of the legal authority Congress gave up.

His use of tariffs also has proven erratic. Last year, for instance, he suddenly imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil because its government had prosecuted his friend, former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro. (The Supreme Court decision struck down that tariff, among others.)

“Trade policy has sort of gone off the rails and has lost a strategic focus,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. “Now, we’re just using tariffs as a blunt cudgel instead of addressing real challenges.”

Trump’s tariff frenzy has lifted the average U.S. tariff from around 2.5% when he returned to the White House in January 2025 to 11.2% now, according to Yale University’s Budget Lab. Tariffs are paid by importers in the United States. And they often pass along the burden to consumers via higher prices. Yale’s Budget Lab estimates that tariffs cost the average U.S. household about $900 a year.

That burden comes at a time when elevated inflation is already pinching family budgets, even more so because Trump’s war with Iran has driven up gasoline prices.

But the Republicans who controlled Congress did nothing to reassert their authority and push back against the president’s aggressive use of tariffs.

Voters largely turned against Trump’s tariffs as they voted in the midterm elections. About two-thirds of U.S. voters said Trump’s tariffs had hurt the national economy or the economy in their area, while only about 2 in 10 said they’d helped, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. Voters who saw a negative impact from the tariffs overwhelmingly supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.

Trump, meanwhile, remains committed to his protectionist agenda.

“President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First, whether in trade negotiations or through an economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to questions from The Associated Press.

Democrats must round up Republican votes to repeal Trump tariffs

As they campaigned this fall, Democrats vowed to cancel some Trump tariffs and curb his legal authority to impose others. Their proposals include repealing the tariffs he levied in July on 60 U.S. trading partners for allegedly failing to do enough to crack down on trade in products made by forced labor. Another would require Congress to approve his tariffs.

Turning their ideas into law will require overcoming a daunting obstacle: Trump’s veto power. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress. Even if Democrats win all the congressional races that are still undecided this year, they won’t have enough votes to override a Trump veto on their own. They will need Republican support.

Can they get it? Their resounding midterms victory makes “a veto-proof vote more possible,” said Majerus, the former trade official and now a partner at King & Spalding. “Are Republicans willing to break with Trump? I’m still skeptical.”

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, sees one issue that could draw Republican support: ending the 50% tariffs that Trump imposed in August on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports.

“That’s what we’re focused on, figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto,” said Wyden, who will be Senate Finance chair when the Democrats take over.

The levies damaged relations with America’s neighbor and longstanding ally, drew retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa and hurt U.S. companies that depend on trade with Canada. “The Canadian tariffs, these tariffs on our allies, are wildly unpopular,” Laing said.

Gellert Global Group, a food importer based in Elizabeth, New Jersey, is contending with Trump tariffs on Canadian cheese.

“We are paying millions of dollars in additional costs and tariffs to maintain our distribution and have our products on the shelf,” said co-CEO Thomas Gellert. “We’re absorbing that today. It’s not sustainable for our business.” The company, represented by the libertarian advocacy group Liberty Justice Center, has sued the Trump administration over the Canada tariffs.

Furor over the Canada tariffs contributed to longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ loss in Maine — even after Trump exempted products from the levies to aid her reelection bid.

Republicans, Wyden said, face a choice: They can “help lower costs for American families or they can continue to defend Trump’s tariffs and make clear whose side they’re on.”

AP Polling Editor Amelia Thomson-Deveaux contributed to this story.

—Paul Wiseman, AP Economics Writer

#10501. Harvard study: Hyperscale data centers collectively power through more electricity than some U.S. states

Hyperscale data centers across the country are using as much electricity as entire states over the course of one year, according to a new study.

And with the majority of that power coming from fossil fuels, those data centers produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2024 to 2025. That’s about three times higher than the emissions from the country’s hyperscale data centers in 2018.

The research adds to a growing understanding of just how much the expansion of AI infrastructure and cloud computing has ramped up both electricity use and fossil fuel production across the country. 

Hyperscale data center secrecy

Though the electricity use and pollution from data centers have come under public scrutiny recently, there has been little peer-reviewed science about data center emissions, says Francesca Dominici, an author of the study, published in Nature Sustainability, and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

To her knowledge, Dominici says, the only peer-reviewed study on greenhouse gas emissions and electricity consumption of hyperscaler data centers is from 2018, years before AI caused data center development to skyrocket. 

Dominici and her co-researchers spent two years investigating hyperscale data centers, which often aren’t publicly transparent about their emissions. 

The researchers used satellite imagery to compile a list of 403 hyperscale data centers, scraped the web for information filed in permits, used remote sensing, and relied on Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) data to calculate emissions based on the mix of power plants around the data centers. 

That effort “tells you about the fact that there is a lot of secrecy about these facilities,” Dominici notes. “Why can’t we just have a database which would tell us where are the facilities, how big they are, what’s the total capacity?”

An underestimate on electricity use

The study found that the country’s hyperscale data centers together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity, in just one year. One terawatt hour can power approximately 90,000 homes. 

That means the hyperscale data center fleet uses as much or more electricity than entire states. Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours of electricity a year. 

Some states use far less, like South Carolina (around 84 Twh), Oregon (60 Twh), and Maine (11 Twh). (States like Texas, California, and Florida use much more electricity; 475, 251, and 248 TWh respectively.)

Those figures surprised Dominici. “It’s something so much bigger that I was actually not even expecting myself,” she says. 

And they’re also likely an underestimate, she adds. The paper focused on electricity use from 2024 to 2025, already making the data a year old. 

“So much more construction and development of hyperscaler data centers has been happening just in the last year,” she says. 

Data centers use dirty grids

To supply all that electricity, these hyperscale data centers are relying mostly on fossil fuels, which make up about 54% of the power mix. That includes natural gas (38%) and coal (15%). 

About a quarter of this electricity also came from grid regions that are dirtier than average, researchers say, where coal-fired power plants dominate. The grids on which these data centers rely “really matter” to their overall impact, Dominici says. 

The research also makes clear, she adds, that “there has been no attention on renewable sources,” Dominici says. Though wind and solar are the cheapest power sources to build, they still don’t offer the same stability without battery storage. Fossil fuels are still the easiest way to get quick, constant, high power. 

Alongside the paper, the researchers are also publishing a website, neverjustabuilding.org, that illustrates the findings. Through that website, the researchers hope to reach those involved in some way in data center development, from the communities where data centers are being built to policymakers to utilities to developers themselves.

This study is just the first step in a series of research efforts to better understand the AI data center boom and its impacts, including not only emissions and energy use but noise, water consumption, and the health impacts of that pollution. (The website allows people to sign up for updates on forthcoming research.)

“This gives us now a framework . . . to start not only tracking,” Dominici says, “but also to really start identifying what we can do and where we should build and how to build, so [data centers] will have less of an impact.”

#10499. Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The best AI humanizer for web content is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. If you need a specific tone, Humanize Max gives you four styles and three lengths in one run. If you already work in QuillBot or Grammarly, their humanizers fit the account you have. GPTinf, Humanize AI and Undetectable AI put an AI check next to the rewrite, and Ahrefs gives you quick variants of a short passage.

To compare them on equal terms, we ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each tool in November 2026. It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.
